title: What happened in Bhopal on the night of 3 December 1984?
subject: histoire
description: On the night of 3 December 1984, a cloud of toxic gas escaped from a pesticide plant and spread over a sleeping city. It was one of the worst industrial disasters in history, and its victims are still waiting for justice.
author: myra-houser

hero.hook: Thirty tons of gas, a city asleep, and thousands of residents who would never wake up.

blocks.text: The Bhopal disaster of **1984** affected millions of people over several years. Court cases and victims' campaigns continue to this day. It began with a chemical leak, one night, at a plant in Bhopal, India. The damage to health and to the environment would last far longer than the leak itself.

Bhopal stands alongside other accidents of the same era: the partial meltdown of the reactor at [[Three Mile Island]], in Pennsylvania, and the explosion at [[Chernobyl]], in Ukraine. Between the late 1970s and the mid-1980s, these accidents made the world aware of the legacy of industrialization, mass production and the Cold War.

sections.title: Bhopal, a large city in central India

blocks.text: Bhopal is a very large city in north-central India. It has even grown since the disaster: nearly **one million** inhabitants in 1984, nearly **two million** today, which places it among the 200 largest cities in the world. Its people are mostly Hindu, with a large Muslim community. Diwali and Eid are the two great festivals of its year.

blocks.caption: The Taj Mahal in Agra, the mausoleum built by Emperor Shah Jahan: the palace in Bhopal borrowed its name.

blocks.text: Less famous than Mumbai or Delhi, the city still receives a fair number of tourists each year. Its great attraction is the Taj Mahal Palace, a huge 19th-century palace that bears the same name as the celebrated mausoleum in Agra. That is no coincidence, but it is not the same builder either.
The Taj Mahal in Agra was the work of Emperor Shah Jahan. The palace in Bhopal was built by another Shah Jahan: the [[begum]] who ruled the city at the time.

sections.title: The Union Carbide plant and MIC gas

blocks.text: In **1969**, [[Union Carbide]] India Limited, the Indian subsidiary of an American group, built a plant near Bhopal. The rise of commercial farming during the [[Green Revolution]] had sent demand for pesticides soaring. The plant produced one of them, Sevin. To make it, it used among other things a gas, [[methyl isocyanate]], MIC for short. Not every factory used it, and those that did followed strict safety protocols.

In the early 1980s, production of Sevin slowed, and MIC built up inside the compound. Between **1976** and **1984**, several MIC leaks occurred inside the facility. During one of them, a worker took off his mask and breathed the gas for a few minutes. He died **72 hours** later.

sections.title: Thirty tons of gas over a sleeping city

blocks.text: On the night of **3 December 1984**, more than **30 tons** of MIC escaped from the facility and spread into the air of Bhopal. The gas has a strong smell, but in the open air it can dissipate, and by the time of the leak most residents were asleep. MIC causes acute lung failure and lasting lung damage; it is also especially dangerous to the eyes and the digestive system.

blocks.caption: A plaque in memory of the thousands killed at Bhopal, in Greyfriars Kirkyard, Edinburgh, Scotland.

blocks.text: The effect on the city was devastating. The death toll has varied over the decades, but an official affidavit from the Indian government, in **2006**, gives several figures. About **3,000** people died in their sleep on 3 December, and about **8,000** in the two weeks that followed. Since then, more than half a million people have suffered disabilities and breathing problems, whether temporary or lasting.

sections.title: Compensation, trials and the memory of the disaster

blocks.text: By the number of people affected, Bhopal is one of the most serious industrial disasters in history. It came after the Three Mile Island accident of **1979** and before Chernobyl in **1986**. These images of technology running out of control marked an era of accelerated industrialization. The disaster still weighs on the lives of survivors, who lost loved ones or suffer from poor health themselves.

blocks.caption: Abdul Jabbar Khan, a campaigner for the Bhopal victims, at his community center in 2013.

blocks.text: In **1989**, Union Carbide reached a settlement with the victims and their families: **$470 million**, spread across several agreements. The company denies having ignored warnings about faulty valves. In the late 1980s, Indian officials tried to charge UCIL's leaders with homicide, but the multinational lay outside their jurisdiction. For an India carried by industrial growth and the Green Revolution, Bhopal revealed the dark side of the promises of industrialization.

blocks.text: On the night of 3 December 1984, more than 30 tons of MIC gas escaping from a Union Carbide pesticide plant killed thousands of Bhopal residents in their sleep and left more than half a million people sick, whose fight for justice is not over.
